paras: The lynching of Bill Young was the hanging of a man by a mob at his home near Luray, Clark County, Missouri, on October 29, 1879, four days after a jury at Kahoka acquitted him of murdering the Spencer family. Wire reports carried the story nationally as a court verdict overturned by a mob, and the alleged leader, detective Frank Lane, was later indicted for murder but released on habeas corpus.

Young was charged with the 1877 murder of Lewis Spencer and four of his family near Luray and bound over in March 1879. During the trial at Kahoka, Lane reported that he had been assaulted and that bloody overalls offered as evidence were missing, and a Keokuk dispatch said that had he died, Young 'would no doubt have been lynched.'

The Tribune and Globe-Democrat correspondents wrote that Lane's 'fiasco' over the overalls weakened the prosecution, but most of Clark County still believed Young guilty. The jury acquitted him on October 25, and the next day he married Lydia Bray of Ohio at Kahoka.

The mob had met at Lincoln College near Kahoka the night before and planned to take Young from the train, but a delayed telegram let it pass. They followed on horseback and in wagons to his house near Luray, about ten miles off, and demanded his surrender.

In the gunfight that followed Young fired from the doorway until he had been wounded four times. The mob piled hay around the house to burn it, but Young's children ran out saying their father was dead, and men entered and brought him out.

Placed in a wagon under an arched orchard gateway beside the house, Young refused, by one account, an offer to spare him if he confessed and left the country. His reported last words were 'I am as innocent of that crime as the angels in heaven.' At four o'clock the wagon was pulled away, and the mob refused his wife's plea to cut him down.

On November 1 Lydia Young swore before a Kahoka justice that about 300 men had killed her husband, naming nine, including Lane. The accused submitted to arrest but refused to go to Kahoka, and when they appeared before a magistrate at Luray on November 5 no one came to prosecute.

Judge Anderson at Memphis, Missouri, then issued bench warrants, and Sheriff Graves of Scotland County pursued the leaders with a posse. Cross and Brown were captured, but the sheriff abandoned the search for Lane, saying it would take 300 men to arrest him in northern Clark County.

In 1880 a Scotland County grand jury indicted Lane for Young's murder, and he was rearrested at Yankton, Dakota Territory, and jailed at Mexico, Missouri. A judge denied his habeas corpus petition in September, but in November 1880 the supreme court discharged him and he left 'for parts unknown.'
A monument to the Spencer family was dedicated in August 1880, and an item about it reported that Young's widow had sued the county for $10,000.

Keokuk dispatches to the Chicago Tribune and St. Louis Globe-Democrat ran nationally on October 30 under headlines such as 'Cleared by Law and Lynched by the People' and 'A Bridegroom Lynched.' The St. Paul Daily Globe's headline compressed the story into 'Acquitted of Murder Saturday Married Sunday and Lynched Monday.' The New York Herald reprinted the full Tribune account on November 3, and dispatches on the arrests ran in Washington and St. Paul.

The detailed accounts treated the belief in Young's guilt as widely shared 'however much they may deprecate lynch law' and called the mob 'good citizens.' A Globe-Democrat letter printed in Memphis revived claims about an older murder in which Young had been convicted, saying it had 'greatly incited the mob.' By 1880 the tone had shifted: the Mexico Weekly Ledger headlined 'Mob Law Must be Put Down' and quoted a Clark County paper calling Lane a 'cold-blooded murderer,' and monument items said little or nothing had been proven against Young.

Estimates of the mob ranged from 100 to 200 men in the Globe-Democrat to 1,300 in the Portland Daily Press, with the widow swearing to about 300. The first dispatches said Young fired first and the Portland version that he wounded eight, while the October 30 dispatch said the first shooter was unknown.

Young was hanged by a mob variously put at 100 to 500 men with no legal authority, four days after his acquittal, because the crowd believed him guilty of the Spencer murders (A11, A16, A20); the papers do not state his race.
Separate Chicago Tribune, Globe-Democrat and later Keokuk dispatches agree on the siege and hanging, and court proceedings against the alleged leader followed (A7, A11, A20, A32).

accounts.gist: A mob of 200 to 300 followed Young home after he left the train; he fired on them and was wounded; eight men took him out and hanged him.

accounts.label: Full Tribune and Globe-Democrat Keokuk accounts
accounts.gist: The mob planned the hanging at Lincoln College, besieged the house near Luray, wounded Young, threatened to burn the house, and hanged him at the orchard gateway at four o'clock after he denied guilt; Lane chose the hangmen.

accounts.label: Keokuk dispatch of Oct. 30
accounts.gist: The first shooter was unknown; the mob offered to spare Young if he confessed, paid costs and left, and he refused to confess; the men wore no masks.

accounts.label: Widow's affidavit
accounts.gist: Lydia Young swore that about 300 men hanged her husband and named nine as present and aiding.

accounts.label: Monument retrospectives (1880)
accounts.gist: Nothing was proven against Young beyond his bad character; the lynchers answered his last words with 'You're a good man to hang, anyhow.'

framing.detail: Wire headlines stressed the irony of acquittal followed by lynching: 'Cleared by Law and Lynched by the People', 'A Bridegroom Lynched', 'Young Yanked'.
The Tribune account said the public shared the belief in Young's guilt 'however much they may deprecate lynch law' and called the mob 'good citizens', while reporting that his friends saw an outrage.
The Mexico Weekly Ledger headlined 'Mob Law Must be Put Down' and quoted a Clark County paper calling Lane a 'cold-blooded murderer'.
Later items called Young 'notorious' and a 'desperado' while saying there was little or no evidence against him; a Globe-Democrat letter revived an older murder charge against him.

conflicts.note: The dispatches dated Oct. 29 say 'to-day' and narrate the couple's Monday arrival at Keokuk first, so the Monday headlines appear to conflate arrival and lynching.
The Portland figure is the outlier; the Tribune account itself gives two ranges.

acts.note: Mob met at Lincoln College the night before and planned to take Young from the train; a delayed telegram let him pass.
Mob and Young exchanged fire at the house; Young hit four times. Who fired first is disputed.
Mob threatened to burn the house.
Hay piled around the house to burn it; children ran out and men entered instead.
Men entered the house and carried the wounded Young to a wagon at the orchard gateway.
Mob offered to spare him if he confessed, paid costs and left the country; he refused (A20 says by one account).
Hanged by pulling the wagon from under him at about four o'clock; Lane picked nine men to hang him; mob refused his wife's plea to cut him down.
